items.title: fastfields
items.text:
fastfields is the Python interface to the fastfields toolkit. In the common case you import one module, fastfields.auto, and call it on whatever array you have: it looks at the array's type, NumPy or PyTorch, and runs the operation on the matching backend. Write your code once and it works across frameworks.

One pip install fastfields gives you all of it: fastfields.auto, the per-framework modules fastfields.numpy, fastfields.torch and fastfields.cupy, and the shared fastfields.helpers. Only the backends you install are loaded, so fastfields[numpy] alone is a perfectly good setup. Today the tested, working path is the CPU one, with NumPy and PyTorch. The CuPy and GPU path is implemented but not yet published as a wheel or validated on hardware; see Status below.

This is the Python section of the fastfields documentation. The project overview has the per-operation status matrix and the roadmap. The layers underneath are documented separately: the raw DLPack binding and the C++/CUDA library.

items.title: Install
items.text:
# CPU (NumPy)
pip install "fastfields[numpy]" \
    --extra-index-url https://fastfields.github.io/whl/cpu/

Use fastfields[torch] for PyTorch, or fastfields[all] for all three.

The extra picks the array library, and the --extra-index-url picks the compiled fastfields-dlpack build. These are two separate choices, and the second one is the one that matters for GPU work; see the packaging note. A GPU wheel lane is planned but not published yet; see Status.

items.title: A first example
items.text:
import numpy as np
from fastfields import auto as ff

feature = np.full((256, 256), np.inf, dtype="float32")
feature[:, 128] = 0.0  # features are 0, everything else is +inf

dist = ff.dt_euclidean(feature)  # dispatched to the NumPy backend

The same call on a torch.Tensor, for instance ff.dt_euclidean(torch.as_tensor(feature)), is dispatched to PyTorch.

items.title: What's inside
items.text:
Operation Functions Distance transforms dt_euclidean and dt_l1; point-to-spline dt_spline_table, dt_spline_brent and dt_spline_gaussnewton; point-to-mesh dt_mesh Positive-definite linear algebra sym_matvec, sym_matvec_backward, sym_solve and sym_invert, over whole fields of small symmetric matrices Resampling resample (spline up- and down-sampling), restriction (its adjoint) and spline_coeff (the coefficient prefilter) Spline sampling (pushpull) pull and push (gather and its adjoint scatter), count and grad: the building blocks of image warping Regularisers field_matvec and flow_matvec (absolute, membrane and bending energies on multi-channel fields and on vector flows) and the operators built on them: diagonals, stencils, accumulate forms, the weighted *_rls variants and the regularised system (H + L) x = g

Each call forwards straight to the selected backend, so it shares that backend's signature and behaviour: autograd on PyTorch, CUDA streams on CuPy. In-place spellings are dispatched too (dt_euclidean_, sym_solve_, spline_coeff_, the *_add…_ and *_sub…_ accumulate forms). They update their first argument, which is also the array the backend is chosen from.

If you only use one framework, import its module directly: fastfields.numpy, fastfields.torch or fastfields.cupy. They are in the same install. What dispatch leaves out is described on the fastfields.auto page.

dt_spline_* returns (dist, time) on every backend

The three point-to-spline operators return a 2-tuple, and all three namespaces return it in that order. fastfields.cupy returned (time, dist) until fastfields#38. A dispatcher that forwards arguments unchanged has nowhere to normalise a result, so the meaning of a dispatched return value depended on which array type you passed. The names are part of the canonical surface that the cross-backend conformance suite checks, so a namespace cannot quietly drift again.

Their signatures agreed later than their return order did. fastfields.cupy spelled the spline order spline and made max_iter, tol and step required positional arguments, where numpy and torch had keyword-only order and bound with defaults. All three now use the numpy and torch spelling, and any drift in parameter names, kinds, order or defaults fails CI in tests/test_signature_conformance.py instead of at a user's call.

items.title: Status
items.text:
fastfields is alpha. The table below is what is actually exposed and tested today, mirroring the candour of the internal migration matrix — so you know before you install.

Operation NumPy (CPU) PyTorch (CPU) CuPy (GPU) Distance — Euclidean / L1 ✅ ✅ 🧭 Distance — point-to-mesh / point-to-spline 🧪 🧪 🧭 Positive-definite linear algebra (sym_*) ✅ ✅ 🧭 Resampling (resample / restriction / spline_coeff) ✅ ✅ 🧭 Pushpull (spline gather / scatter / grad) ✅ ✅ 🧭 Regularisers (membrane / bending energies) ✅ ✅ 🧭

✅ works, covered by the CPU test suite  ·  🧪 exposed but not yet covered by tests (shape contracts still being firmed up — use with care)  ·  🧭 planned (see below).

What "planned" means here:

  • GPU / CuPy (the only remaining 🧭). The CUDA kernels and the CuPy wrapper exist and compile + link — every op family, pushpull and the regularisers included, is exposed on all three backends — but there is no GPU in CI, so no GPU wheel is published yet and nothing has run on real hardware. The wheel lanes are deferred until that changes.

Everything marked ✅ is exercised by a brute-force reference test on CPU.

See the API reference for full signatures and options, and one distribution, five namespaces for how the packaging fits together.

items.title: fastfields.auto
items.text:
fastfields.auto dispatches on the array type. Each function looks at the type of its first array argument and forwards the call, unchanged, to the matching per-framework package. Write the call once and it runs on whichever array library the caller happens to use.

you pass it calls numpy.ndarray fastfields.numpy torch.Tensor fastfields.torch cupy.ndarray fastfields.cupy

items.title: Install
items.text:
pip install "fastfields[numpy]" \
    --extra-index-url https://fastfields.github.io/whl/cpu/

fastfields.auto ships with the fastfields distribution and has no extra of its own. It has nothing to dispatch to until at least one backend is installed, so pick the extra for the array library you use ([numpy], [torch], [cupy] or [all]). It then dispatches over exactly the subset you installed.

items.title: A first example
items.text:
import numpy as np
from fastfields import auto as ff

feature = np.full((256, 256), np.inf, dtype="float32")
feature[:, 128] = 0.0  # features are 0, everything else is +inf

dist = ff.dt_euclidean(feature)  # runs on fastfields.numpy

Hand the same function a torch.Tensor and it runs on fastfields.torch instead, with autograd, and returns a tensor. Arguments are forwarded unchanged, so each call has the signature of the backend function it selects. Spline orders and boundary conditions accept an int, a Spline or Bound member, or a name such as "cubic" or "dct2", exactly as they do on a concrete backend.

items.title: When to use it
items.text:
Reach for fastfields.auto when the array type is not yours to choose: library code that must accept whatever its caller passes, a function that runs over both NumPy and PyTorch data, or a script you want to move between CPU and GPU without rewriting imports.

When you already know the array type, import the backend directly: fastfields.numpy, fastfields.torch or fastfields.cupy. You get the backend's own documented signatures, and a problem with the installation shows up when you import it, not at the first call. Nothing is lost by doing so. fastfields.auto adds dispatch, not capability: every operation it reaches is one of those three already has.

items.title: Backends are imported lazily
items.text:
The backend is chosen from the top-level module name of the array's type, so importing fastfields.auto does not import NumPy, PyTorch or CuPy. Only the backend of an array you actually pass is imported, and only once. That is what makes the package usable with any subset of them installed.

The failures are specific:

  • an object that is not a NumPy, PyTorch or CuPy array raises TypeError, naming the type it was given;
  • an array whose backend package, or that package's own dependency, is not installed raises ImportError, naming what to install;
  • an operation that a backend does not have raises NotImplementedError, naming the backends that do, and never a bare AttributeError from a module the caller did not mention.

items.title: What is not dispatched
items.text:
Two kinds of operation cannot be reached through fastfields.auto, and both are deliberate.

  • Builders that take a shape, not an array. field_diag, flow_diag, field_kernel and flow_kernel allocate their output from a rank or shape and a set of penalty weights, so there is no array to dispatch on. Call them on a concrete backend and pass the result to the dispatched operators. Their *_add… and *_sub… accumulate forms do take an array and are dispatched.
  • Adjoints that exist for autograd. pull_backward, push_backward, count_backward and grad_backward are wired into the autograd.Function of fastfields.torch instead of being exported, since only PyTorch has an autograd engine. The supported spelling is fastfields.auto.pull(...) followed by .backward() on a torch tensor.

A few operations exist on some backends only. They are dispatched with a partial table and raise NotImplementedError naming the backends that have them: field_cg (numpy only), field_precond_ and flow_precond_ (numpy and cupy), and sym_matvec_backward (numpy and cupy). Listing them with a clear failure keeps the asymmetry visible.

items.title: Which lane am I on?
items.text:
fastfields.auto never requires a particular compute backend. By contrast, fastfields.cupy refuses to import on a CPU-only build, and fastfields.torch refuses a CUDA tensor on one. fastfields.auto only reports:

from fastfields import auto as ff

ff.dlpack_backend()  # "cpu", "cu126", ... or None

None means that the installed fastfields-dlpack carries no lane label, or that it cannot be imported at all. Only the CPU lane is published today, so fastfields.cupy and CUDA torch tensors are not usable yet. See the project status matrix.

The API reference lists every dispatched operation and the backend page that documents it.

items.title: fastfields.cupy
items.text:
fastfields.cupy runs the fastfields operators on the GPU, directly on CuPy arrays. The API is the one of fastfields.numpy, but the work happens in device memory and is ordered on CuPy's current CUDA stream.

CuPy itself is not installed automatically, because the right build depends on your CUDA version. Install it with the cupy extra, or install a matching build such as cupy-cuda12x yourself.

items.title: Install
items.text:
pip install "fastfields[cupy]" \
    --extra-index-url https://fastfields.github.io/whl/cu130/

The extra selects CuPy; the index URL selects the CUDA kernels

These are two separate choices, and only the second one can fail quietly. pip install "fastfields[cupy]" installs CuPy and succeeds even against a CPU-only fastfields-dlpack, because pip has no way to say "any build with CUDA": the lane comes from the index folder you point it at. import fastfields.cupy then fails at once, with a message naming the lane to install, because there is no CPU path to fall back to. See the packaging note for why it works this way.

No cu* lane is published yet. Until one is, this install has nothing to resolve to. The wheel index lists the lanes that exist.

items.title: A first example
items.text:
import cupy as cp
import fastfields.cupy as ff

feature = cp.full((256, 256), cp.inf, dtype="float32")
feature[:, 128] = 0.0  # features are 0, everything else is +inf

dist = ff.dt_euclidean(feature)  # a new array; feature is untouched
ff.dt_euclidean_(feature)  # the in-place variant writes into feature

items.title: What's inside
items.text:
Operation Functions Distance transforms dt_euclidean and dt_l1 along the last axis; point-to-spline dt_spline_table, dt_spline_brent and dt_spline_gaussnewton; point-to-mesh dt_mesh Positive-definite linear algebra sym_matvec, sym_addmatvec_, sym_submatvec_, sym_solve and sym_invert, over whole fields of small symmetric matrices Resampling resample (spline up- and down-sampling), restriction (its adjoint) and spline_coeff (the coefficient prefilter) Spline sampling (pushpull) pull (gather), push (scatter), count and grad Regularisers field_* for a multi-channel field, with one penalty per channel, and flow_* for a vector flow, with scalar penalties plus the Lamé shears and div terms. Each family has the operator (*_matvec), its diagonal (*_diag), its stencil (*_kernel), accumulate forms of each (*_add… and *_sub…), weighted variants (*_rls) and the regularised system described below

The functions without a trailing underscore allocate their outputs and return new arrays. The ones with a trailing underscore (dt_euclidean_, sym_solve_ and so on) write in place. To run on a specific stream, call the function inside a with my_stream: block.

A field is a multi-channel array with any number of channels. A flow is a vector field whose number of channels equals the number of spatial dimensions. The regularisers act on the ndim axes just before the channel axis, and ndim is not inferred: it defaults to 1, so pass ndim=2 for a 2D image.

items.title: Solving the regularised system
items.text:
Let H be the per-voxel Hessian of a data term, stored as compact-symmetric matrices, and L a regulariser. These functions apply and solve the system (H + L) x = g:

call what it does field_forward, flow_forward apply (H + L) x field_precond, flow_precond apply (H + diag(L))⁻¹ g, the Jacobi preconditioner field_precond_, flow_precond_ the same, in place field_relax, flow_relax Gauss-Seidel sweeps on the system

Each of these is a single fused kernel, so none of them allocates a temporary that you would then have to keep alive until the stream is synchronised.

items.title: What this package does not wrap
items.text:
Of the 58 operations of the underlying C++ library, this package wraps all but five.

pull_backward, push_backward, count_backward and grad_backward are the adjoints of the sampling operators with respect to both the sampled field and the sampling coordinates. They exist so that an autograd engine can differentiate through grid, which only fastfields.torch does. CuPy has no automatic differentiation, so they stay at the raw layer, as fastfields.dlpack.pull_backward(...) and so on.

field_cg, the conjugate-gradient solver, is CPU-only in the underlying library. Its dot products need a device-side reduction that the CUDA backend does not implement yet (fastfields-lib#34), and the hub rejects CUDA arrays instead of quietly running on the host. A fastfields.cupy.field_cg could therefore only ever raise, so there isn't one. Use field_relax, which runs on CUDA and solves the same system by Gauss-Seidel sweeps.

tests/test_api_coverage_cupy.py fails if that list ever changes by accident, and it runs without a GPU.

See the API reference for the full signatures.

items.title: fastfields.helpers
items.text: fastfields.helpers is the part of the fastfields stack that does not depend on an array library. It holds the Spline and Bound enums and the helpers that turn user-friendly arguments into what the compiled library expects. It is shared by fastfields.numpy, fastfields.torch, fastfields.cupy and the fastfields.auto dispatcher.

items.title: Install
items.text:
pip install fastfields

It ships with the fastfields distribution, so there is nothing extra to install. The module imports only the standard library: no array backend and none of the compiled bindings.

items.title: A first example
items.text:
from fastfields.helpers import Bound, Spline, as_bound, as_spline

as_spline("cubic")  # 3
as_bound("wrap")  # 6, which is int(Bound.DFT)
as_spline(Spline.Linear)  # 1

The normalisers are what let every order and bound argument in the other namespaces accept an int, an enum member or a name.

items.title: What's inside
items.text: Group Names Enums Spline (orders 0 to 7) and Bound (eight boundary conditions) Normalisers as_spline and as_bound accept an int, an enum member or a name Shapes normalize_shape, infer_ndim, check_ndim and resolve_out_spatial work out the arguments of a resampling call Anchors anchor_scale_shift turns an interpol.resize anchor into a per-axis scale and a scalar shift Compute backend is_cuda_backend and cuda_backend_message decide whether the installed fastfields-dlpack is a CUDA build, and word the error when it is not

items.title: Why it is a separate namespace
items.text:
These helpers used to live inside fastfields-dlpack, next to the compiled extension. A one-line fix to a string alias or a rounding rule could then only reach users through a full compiled-wheel release on every platform. They were split out to escape that, and the escape survives the merge into one distribution: fastfields is still a single universal py3-none-any wheel with no compiled content, so fixing a helper is an ordinary pure-Python release.

For the same reason the module must keep depending on nothing. It imports no array library and, in particular, never fastfields.dlpack; a subprocess test enforces that.

See the API reference for the full signatures.

items.title: One distribution, five namespaces
items.text:
fastfields used to be five separate PyPI distributions, one for each subpackage of the fastfields namespace. It is now one distribution that ships all five. The import surface did not move: the same fastfields.<sub> modules exist with the same contents, and fastfields.dlpack still merges into the same namespace from its own wheel.

was shipped now fastfields-helpers fastfields.helpers fastfields fastfields-numpy fastfields.numpy fastfields fastfields-cupy fastfields.cupy fastfields fastfields-torch fastfields.torch fastfields fastfields fastfields.auto fastfields fastfields-dlpack fastfields.dlpack fastfields-dlpack (unchanged)

items.title: What stayed the same, on purpose
items.text:
The subpackages are still PEP 420 namespace subpackages. There is no fastfields/__init__.py anywhere, in this distribution or in fastfields-dlpack, and that absence is the whole mechanism. fastfields is a native namespace package, so two independently installed wheels can each contribute a fastfields/<sub>/ directory and both stay importable. Add a top-level __init__.py and fastfields becomes an ordinary package owned by whichever wheel shipped it, and fastfields.dlpack, the compiled half, stops being importable. For this reason the merged pyproject.toml lists each subpackage explicitly with namespaces = true, and tools/consolidate-python.sh fails if an __init__.py ever appears there.

fastfields-dlpack stays a separate distribution and repository. It is the only compiled one. It needs a per-platform wheel matrix, and libfastfields-cpu.so alone is about 166 MB. Folding it in would mean that every one-line Python fix rebuilds and re-uploads that whole matrix, which is exactly why fastfields-helpers was split out of it in the first place. Merging the five pure-Python distributions keeps that property: fastfields is still one universal py3-none-any wheel with no compiled content, so a fix to any of the five ships as an ordinary pure-Python release. There is no circularity either, because fastfields-dlpack depends only on packaging and never on anything here.

The array libraries are still optional. numpy, torch and cupy are extras (fastfields[numpy], [torch], [cupy] and [all]), so pip install fastfields works with whatever subset you have, and fastfields.auto dispatches over exactly that subset. fastfields-dlpack is the only hard dependency.

items.title: The one wrinkle: an extra is not a lane
items.text:
Read this before filing a bug.

fastfields-dlpack records the compute backend it was compiled for in the local segment of its PEP 440 version, in the PyTorch style: 0.0.dev0+cpu, +cu118, +cu126, +cu130. At runtime that is fastfields.dlpack.backend. Which one you get is decided by the index folder you install from, not by the dependency graph:

pip install fastfields --extra-index-url https://fastfields.github.io/whl/cpu/
pip install fastfields --extra-index-url https://fastfields.github.io/whl/cu130/

No package in this distribution pins a lane, and none can. pip has no way to express "any build with CUDA", and a pin would fight the --extra-index-url you just chose. So the dependency on fastfields-dlpack is deliberately unqualified.

The consequence is that the cupy extra selects the CuPy client library, not the CUDA lane:

pip install "fastfields[cupy]"  # succeeds, on the CPU lane too
python -c "import fastfields.cupy"  # ImportError

That install is not wrong in any way pip can see, and it is not a resolution failure. It is a mismatch that only the package itself can detect, so each namespace enforces its own requirement at runtime:

namespace needs what it does fastfields.numpy CPU Nothing. The CPU path works on any build. fastfields.cupy CUDA Fails at import if fastfields.dlpack.backend is not cu*. Every operation runs in CUDA device memory, so there is no partial mode worth offering. The message names the index URL and the pip command. fastfields.torch either Fails lazily. The CPU path is the tested one and runs on any build, so the import always succeeds and the check happens only when a CUDA tensor arrives, in stream_ptr, which every operation already calls. fastfields.auto whatever is installed Reports. fastfields.auto.dlpack_backend() returns the label, and dispatch is dynamic already.

An unlabelled build (backend is None, which is what an unversioned source checkout reports) is let through everywhere. It means unknown, not CPU, and every wheel from the index carries a real label, so refusing it would block GPU development from a source tree while catching no real mistake.

items.title: How the merge was done
items.text:
tools/consolidate-python.sh is the frozen record. It is the Python-side sibling of tools/consolidate.sh in fastfields-lib. In outline there was one git filter-repo path-move pass for each absorbed repository, followed by four --allow-unrelated-histories merges into this repository's existing history. This repository was not rewritten, so its main is still a true ancestor of the result and every existing commit SHA and permalink against it still resolves.

History is preserved across the old fastfields_numpy/ to fastfields/numpy/ layout rename too, which the path rules fold onto one path so that git log --follow crosses it. Issue and PR numbers do not transfer, because GitHub does not redirect them across a repository merge. A reference to, say, fastfields-numpy#23 remains a reference to that archived repository.

items.title: fastfields.numpy
items.text: fastfields.numpy runs the fastfields operators on NumPy arrays, on the CPU. Arrays go in and freshly allocated arrays come out. Your inputs are left alone unless you call one of the in-place variants, whose names end in an underscore.

items.title: Install
items.text:
pip install "fastfields[numpy]" \
    --extra-index-url https://fastfields.github.io/whl/cpu/

The numpy extra installs NumPy itself. The --extra-index-url is what selects the compiled fastfields-dlpack build, and cpu is the right one here. The same fastfields distribution also ships fastfields.torch, fastfields.cupy, fastfields.auto and fastfields.helpers.

items.title: A first example
items.text:
import numpy as np
import fastfields.numpy as ff

feature = np.full((256, 256), np.inf, dtype="float32")
feature[:, 128] = 0.0  # features are 0, everything else is +inf

dist = ff.dt_euclidean(feature)  # squared distance to column 128, per row

Distance transforms work along the last axis and expect 0 at the features and +inf elsewhere. dt_euclidean returns squared distances.

items.title: What's inside
items.text:
Operation Functions Distance transforms dt_euclidean and dt_l1 along the last axis; point-to-spline dt_spline_table, dt_spline_brent and dt_spline_gaussnewton; point-to-mesh dt_mesh Positive-definite linear algebra sym_matvec, sym_addmatvec_, sym_submatvec_, sym_solve and sym_invert, over whole fields of small symmetric matrices Resampling resample (spline up- and down-sampling), restriction (its adjoint) and spline_coeff (the coefficient prefilter) Spline sampling (pushpull) pull (gather), push (scatter), count and grad Regularisers field_* for a multi-channel field, with one penalty per channel, and flow_* for a vector flow, with scalar penalties plus the Lamé shears and div terms. Each family has the operator (*_matvec), its diagonal (*_diag), its stencil (*_kernel), accumulate forms of each (*_add… and *_sub…), weighted variants (*_rls) and the regularised system described below

Anything that selects a spline order or a boundary condition (order, bound) accepts an int, a Spline or Bound member, or a name such as "cubic" or "dct2".

A field is a multi-channel array with any number of channels. A flow is a vector field whose number of channels equals the number of spatial dimensions. The regularisers act on the ndim axes just before the channel axis, and ndim is not inferred: it defaults to 1, so pass ndim=2 for a 2D image.

items.title: Solving the regularised system
items.text:
Let H be the per-voxel Hessian of a data term, stored as compact-symmetric matrices, and L a regulariser. These functions apply and solve the system (H + L) x = g:

call what it does field_forward, flow_forward apply (H + L) x field_precond, flow_precond apply (H + diag(L))⁻¹ g, the Jacobi preconditioner field_precond_, flow_precond_ the same, in place field_relax, flow_relax Gauss-Seidel sweeps on the system field_cg preconditioned conjugate gradients on the same system

field_cg updates sol in place and returns it, like field_relax. Pass return_info=True to also get the iteration count and the final relative residual. The solver is CPU-only in the underlying library, which is why fastfields.cupy has no field_cg.

items.title: Batch axes and memory
items.text: Leading axes are batch axes, and they broadcast: you can combine a single matrix field with a stack of vector fields, and the result carries the broadcast batch shape. The broadcast is a view with zero strides, so nothing is copied. Inputs are likewise passed with their own strides instead of being made contiguous. Only read-only arrays are copied, because NumPy cannot export them through DLPack.

items.title: What this package does not wrap
items.text:
Of the 58 operations of the underlying C++ library, this package wraps all but four: pull_backward, push_backward, count_backward and grad_backward. They are the adjoints of the sampling operators with respect to both the sampled field and the sampling coordinates, and they exist so that an autograd engine can differentiate through grid. Only fastfields.torch has one, so NumPy has no use for them. They stay at the raw layer, as fastfields.dlpack.pull_backward(...) and so on. tests/test_api_coverage_numpy.py fails if that list ever changes by accident.

See the API reference for the full signatures.

items.title: fastfields.torch
items.text: fastfields.torch runs the fastfields operators on PyTorch tensors, and most of them are differentiable: put them inside a model and gradients flow straight through. Functions take tensors and return newly allocated tensors.

items.title: Install
items.text:
pip install "fastfields[torch]" \
    --extra-index-url https://fastfields.github.io/whl/cpu/

CPU tensors work with any build of fastfields-dlpack. A CUDA tensor needs a CUDA build, which means installing from one of the cu* lanes of the index instead of cpu/; then the same code runs on the GPU. Handing a CUDA tensor to a CPU-only build raises a RuntimeError that names the lane to install. The check happens when the tensor arrives and not at import, so the CPU path keeps working everywhere.

items.title: A first example
items.text:
import torch
import fastfields.torch as ff

mat = torch.randn(5, 6, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)  # packed, C=3
vec = torch.randn(5, 3, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)

out = ff.sym_matvec(mat, vec)  # H @ vec, one 3x3 matrix per row
out.sum().backward()  # gradients land on both mat and vec

items.title: What's inside
items.text:
Operation Functions Positive-definite linear algebra sym_matvec and sym_solve (differentiable); sym_invert, sym_addmatvec_ and sym_submatvec_, over whole fields of small symmetric matrices Resampling resample (spline up- and down-sampling), restriction (its adjoint) and spline_coeff (the coefficient prefilter), all differentiable Spline sampling (pushpull) pull, push, count and grad, all differentiable with respect to the sampling grid Distance transforms dt_euclidean, dt_l1, dt_mesh and point-to-spline dt_spline_table, dt_spline_brent and dt_spline_gaussnewton Regularisers field_* for a multi-channel field, with one penalty per channel, and flow_* for a vector flow, with scalar penalties plus the Lamé shears and div terms. Each family has the operator (*_matvec), its diagonal (*_diag), its stencil (*_kernel), accumulate forms of each (*_add… and *_sub…), weighted variants (*_rls), *_relax, and *_forward and *_precond

A field is a multi-channel tensor with any number of channels. A flow is a vector field whose number of channels equals the number of spatial dimensions. The regularisers act on the ndim axes just before the channel axis, and ndim is not inferred: it defaults to 1, so pass ndim=2 for a 2D image.

items.title: What is differentiable
items.text:
These operations support .backward():

  • sym_matvec, with respect to mat and vec, and sym_solve, with respect to vec only (mat must not require grad);
  • resample, restriction and spline_coeff, with respect to the input;
  • all four sampling operators, with respect to the field and the sampling coordinates (count only has the coordinates);
  • the regulariser operators, including field_forward and field_precond and their flow twins.

grad deserves a remark. It is itself a derivative operator, so differentiating it produces second-order terms. That is the point: an image gradient computed inside a loss has to be differentiable for the deformation that produced grid to be learnable. Its abs=True mode is a majorisation, and its backward pass is the adjoint of the majorised operator, not a true Jacobian. Use it as the majorisation it is.

The remaining operations are exposed for parity with fastfields.numpy and fastfields.cupy but are not differentiable: the distance transforms (dt_euclidean, dt_l1, dt_mesh and the three dt_spline_*), sym_invert, the iterative solvers field_relax and flow_relax with their weighted variants, and the gradients of sym_addmatvec_ and sym_submatvec_ with respect to mat and vec. Their forward pass always runs, even when an input requires grad. Only calling .backward() through the output raises a RuntimeError that names the operation.

items.title: What this package does not wrap
items.text:
Of the 58 operations of the underlying C++ library, this package wraps all but eight, in two groups.

Adjoints that are used, not re-exported. pull_backward, push_backward, count_backward, grad_backward and sym_matvec_backward are the gradients behind the autograd.Function of each forward operation. The supported way to reach them is to call the forward operation and then .backward(). Re-exporting them would be a second, unchecked spelling of a gradient, with pre-zeroed buffers and an accumulate-or-overwrite contract for the caller to get right. fastfields.dlpack has them raw.

Three solver entry points that need an autograd decision first. field_precond_ and flow_precond_ are in-place preconditioner solves, and field_cg runs an iterative solver whose gradient is a solve with the same operator. Both are worth doing and neither is a mechanical wrapper, so they are not here yet. field_relax is the in-place solver available today, and fastfields.numpy has all three for the case without autograd.

tests/test_api_coverage_torch.py fails if that list ever changes by accident.

See the API reference for the full signatures.

items.title: API reference
items.text:
The fastfields distribution ships five subpackages of the fastfields namespace. Pick the one that matches the arrays you work with, or use fastfields.auto and let it choose.

Page Module For auto fastfields.auto dispatches on the type of the array you pass numpy fastfields.numpy NumPy arrays, on the CPU torch fastfields.torch PyTorch tensors, with autograd cupy fastfields.cupy CuPy arrays in CUDA device memory helpers fastfields.helpers the Spline and Bound enums and the argument normalisers

The raw bindings that all of them are built on, fastfields.dlpack, ship from a separate distribution (fastfields-dlpack) and are documented there.

items.title: fastfields.auto
items.text:
fastfields.auto adds dispatch, not new operations. Each function in the tables below forwards to the function of the same name in the backend that matches the type of its first array argument, and has that function's signature, so an operation is documented on the page of its backend. The overview explains how the dispatch works.

A backend is listed for an operation when it implements it. Calling an operation on an array whose backend is not listed raises NotImplementedError naming the backends that are.

items.title: The module
items.text: The module itself, with dlpack_backend and the re-exported enums:

items.title: fastfields.auto
items.text:
Backend-dispatching interface to the fastfields operators.

Every function here looks at the type of its first array argument and forwards the call, unchanged, to the function of the same name in the matching backend:

  • numpy.ndarray: fastfields.numpy
  • torch.Tensor: fastfields.torch
  • cupy.ndarray: fastfields.cupy

Arguments and results pass through untouched, so a dispatched call has the signature of the backend function it selects. The reference page for each operation is the one of its backend; this page documents what is specific to dispatching.

Backends are imported lazily, and only when an array of their type is passed. The package therefore works with any subset of them installed. Its only hard dependency is fastfields.helpers; apart from dlpack_backend, which imports the compiled fastfields-dlpack bindings when it is called, it does not touch them. An object of any other type raises TypeError, and a backend whose package is missing raises ImportError naming what to install.

This namespace does not need any particular compute backend. dlpack_backend reports which one is installed ("cpu", "cu126" and so on). By contrast, fastfields.cupy refuses to import on a CPU-only build and fastfields.torch refuses a CUDA tensor on one.

What is not dispatched here, and why

Two kinds of operation cannot be reached through this module, and both are deliberate.

Builders that take a shape, not an array. field_diag, flow_diag, field_kernel and flow_kernel allocate their output from a rank and a set of penalty weights, so there is no array to dispatch on. Call them on a concrete backend, for example fastfields.numpy.field_diag(...), and pass the result to the dispatched operators. The *_add* and *_sub* accumulate forms take an array and are dispatched.

Adjoints that exist for autograd. pull_backward, push_backward, count_backward and grad_backward are the gradients of the sampling operators. Only PyTorch has an autograd engine, and there they are wired into the forward operation instead of being exported. The supported spelling is fastfields.auto.pull(...) followed by .backward() on a torch tensor, or fastfields.dlpack.pull_backward(...) for the raw function.

Some operations exist on only some backends. They are dispatched with a partial table, and calling one on another backend raises NotImplementedError naming the backends that have it: field_cg (numpy only, because it is CPU-only in the C++ library), field_precond_ and flow_precond_ (numpy and cupy) and sym_matvec_backward (numpy and cupy). Listing them with a clear failure keeps the asymmetry visible.

If a backend lacks an operation that this module says it has, which points to a stale or partial installation, the call raises NotImplementedError saying so, not a bare AttributeError from a module the caller never named.

items.text: Every function of fastfields.cupy, with its arguments, options and exceptions. The overview explains the conventions they share and what this package needs to import.

items.title: fastfields.cupy
items.text:
CuPy interface to the fastfields operators, on the GPU.

The package mirrors fastfields.numpy, but its arrays are CuPy arrays living in CUDA device memory. They reach the compiled library through DLPack, which shares the device memory instead of copying it.

Functions take CuPy arrays and return newly allocated CuPy arrays. Inputs must be float32 or float64 and are passed with their own strides, so nothing is made contiguous; outputs are allocated contiguous. Functions whose name ends in an underscore (dt_euclidean_, sym_solve_ and so on) update their first argument in place and return it.

All work is queued on CuPy's current CUDA stream: every wrapper forwards cupy.cuda.get_current_stream().ptr to the library, so the kernels are ordered with respect to the surrounding CuPy operations. To run on another stream, call the function inside a with my_stream: block.

Availability

Two things can be missing, and they are treated differently.

CuPy itself is imported lazily, so import fastfields.cupy succeeds where CuPy is not installed or there is no GPU; a clear ImportError is raised only when a wrapper is called. That keeps the static parts of the package, the enums and the argument normalisers, importable and testable anywhere.

The CUDA kernels are checked eagerly instead. import fastfields.cupy raises ImportError when the installed fastfields-dlpack is a CPU-only build, and the message names the wheel-index lane to install. Without the kernels nothing here can work, so there is no point in waiting for the first call.

What this wrapper deliberately does not expose

Of the 58 public operations of the C++ hub, this package wraps all but five.

The adjoints of the sampling operators. pull_backward, push_backward, count_backward and grad_backward give the gradient with respect to both the sampled field and the sampling coordinates. They exist so that an autograd engine can differentiate through grid, and only fastfields.torch has one. A wrapper here would be a function that nothing calls, with several pre-zeroed device buffers for the caller to get right. They remain available as fastfields.dlpack.pull_backward(...) and so on.

The conjugate-gradient solver. field_cg is CPU-only in the C++ library: its dot products need a device-side reduction that the CUDA backend does not implement yet (fastfields-lib#34), and the hub rejects CUDA arrays instead of quietly running on the host. A fastfields.cupy.field_cg could therefore only ever raise. field_relax and flow_relax run on CUDA and solve the same system by Gauss-Seidel sweeps.

tests/test_api_coverage_cupy.py fails if the set of omitted operations ever changes by accident.

flow_matvec_rls(inp: Any, wgt: Any, absolute: float = 0.0, membrane: float = 0.0, bending: float = 0.0, shears: float = 0.0, div: float = 0.0, *, voxel_size=None, bound: int | str = 'dct2', ndim: int = 1) -> Any

Apply the weighted (RLS/JRLS) flow regulariser.

The reweighted form of flow_matvec. The weight map wgt modulates the strength of the penalties voxel by voxel, for edge-preserving or robust regularisation. Flow weighting is always joint: one weight per voxel, shared by all flow components. bending is not supported with weighting, and a non-zero value is rejected.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default inp ndarray

The flow to filter, shape (*batch, *spatial, ndim).

required wgt ndarray

Weight map, shape (*batch, *spatial, 1): one weight per voxel, shared by all flow components.

required absolute float

Weight of the absolute (L2) penalty.

0.0 membrane float

Weight of the membrane (first-order) penalty.

0.0 bending float

Weight of the bending (second-order) penalty.

0.0 shears float

Weight of the linear-elastic shear penalty (Lamé mu). Together with div it couples the flow components.

0.0 div float

Weight of the linear-elastic divergence penalty (Lamé lambda).

0.0 voxel_size float or sequence of float

Spatial voxel size: one value per spatial axis, or a single value for all. None means unit voxels.

None bound int or str

Boundary condition: an integer from 0 to 7, a Bound member, or a name such as "dct2" or "wrap".

"dct2" ndim int

Number of spatial axes. They are the ndim axes just before the channel axis; this is not inferred, so pass it explicitly for anything but 1D data.

1

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

The filtered result, a new array the shape of inp.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If an argument is not a float32 or float64 CuPy array.

flow_precond(mat: Any, vec: Any, absolute: float = 0.0, membrane: float = 0.0, bending: float = 0.0, shears: float = 0.0, div: float = 0.0, *, voxel_size=None, bound: int | str = 'dct2', ndim: int = 1) -> Any

Jacobi preconditioner of the regularised system.

Solves (M + diag(L)) x = vec voxel by voxel, where M is the per-voxel matrix mat and diag(L) is the diagonal of the flow regulariser L. It approximates the inverse of the operator of flow_forward. The penalties are scalars. A non-zero shears or div adds the linear-elastic terms, which couple the flow components.

Batch axes of mat and vec are broadcast against each other; the spatial axes and the last axis must match.

flow_precond_ is the in-place version.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mat ndarray

Per-voxel matrix M in compact-symmetric packing, shape (*batch, *spatial, ndim*(ndim+1)//2). Batch axes are broadcast against those of vec.

required vec ndarray

Right-hand side, shape (*batch, *spatial, ndim). Batch axes are broadcast against those of mat.

required absolute float

Weight of the absolute (L2) penalty.

0.0 membrane float

Weight of the membrane (first-order) penalty.

0.0 bending float

Weight of the bending (second-order) penalty.

0.0 shears float

Weight of the linear-elastic shear penalty (Lamé mu). Together with div it couples the flow components.

0.0 div float

Weight of the linear-elastic divergence penalty (Lamé lambda).

0.0 voxel_size float or sequence of float

Spatial voxel size: one value per spatial axis, or a single value for all. None means unit voxels.

None bound int or str

Boundary condition: an integer from 0 to 7, a Bound member, or a name such as "dct2" or "wrap".

"dct2" ndim int

Number of spatial axes. They are the ndim axes just before the channel axis; this is not inferred, so pass it explicitly for anything but 1D data.

1

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

The solution x, shape (*batch, *spatial, ndim) with the broadcast batch shape.

items.title: resample
items.text:
resample(inp: Any, factor: float | Sequence[float] | None = None, shape: int | Sequence[int] | None = None, *, order: int | str = 2, bound: int | str = 'dct2', ndim: Optional[int] = None, anchor: str = 'centers', shift: Optional[float] = None, scale: Optional[Sequence[float]] = None) -> Any

Resample the trailing axes of an array with splines.

Resamples inp onto a new grid with splines of order order, along the last ndim axes; leading axes are batch axes. Give either a size factor or an explicit output shape, not both.

Which points of the two grids line up is set by anchor; with "centers", the default, the first and last samples coincide. The anchor determines the sampling scale and shift for the kernel, and either can be overridden.

restriction is the adjoint operation.

Interpolating resize

resample does not prefilter its input. For a true interpolating resize, pass the coefficients computed by spline_coeff instead of the raw samples.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default inp ndarray

Input, shape (*batch, *spatial_in); the last ndim axes are resampled.

required factor float or sequence of float

Size multiplier, one per resampled axis or a single value for all. Exclusive with shape; with neither, the spatial shape is unchanged. Each output size is max(1, round(n * factor)).

None shape int or sequence of int

Output spatial size, one per resampled axis or a single value for all. Exclusive with factor.

None order int or str

Spline order: an integer from 0 to 7, a Spline member, or a name such as "cubic".

2 bound int or str

Boundary condition: an integer from 0 to 7, a Bound member, or a name such as "dct2" or "wrap".

"dct2" ndim int

Number of trailing axes to resample. When omitted it is the length of shape or factor if either is a sequence, and 1 otherwise.

None anchor ('centers', 'edges', 'first', 'last')

Which points of the input and output grids are aligned; the initial letter is enough. See anchor_scale_shift for the exact scale and shift each choice implies.

"centers" shift float

Sampling shift, replacing the one implied by anchor.

None scale sequence of float

Input-index step per output-index step, one value per resampled axis, replacing the one derived from anchor and the shapes.

None

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

The resampled array, shape (*batch, *spatial_out).

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If ndim is outside 1..inp.ndim, anchor is unknown, or factor, shape or scale has the wrong length.

TypeError

If inp is not a float32 or float64 CuPy array.

Adjoint of resample, along the trailing axes of an array.

Transposes the linear map of resample for the same arguments: values on the finer grid are accumulated onto the coarser one. The scale is derived from this call's own input and output shapes, so a resample and a restriction with matching shapes use reciprocal scales and the same shift.

The binding accumulates into its output buffer, which is why the buffer is allocated zero-filled here. When calling fastfields.dlpack.restriction yourself, pre-zero out.

factor, shape, order, bound, ndim, anchor, shift and scale are exactly as for resample.

items.title: spline_coeff
items.text:
spline_coeff(inp: Any, order: int | str = 3, bound: int | str = 'dct2') -> Any

Spline coefficients of a signal, along the last axis.

Converts samples into the coefficients of the interpolating spline of order order, so that evaluating that spline at the sample positions gives the samples back. For orders 0 and 1 the coefficients are the samples. Only the last axis is filtered.

For orders above 1 only the boundary conditions dct1, dct2, dft and replicate are implemented; any other is rejected. The coefficients are what pull, push and grad expect as their volume.

spline_coeff_ is the in-place version.

3 bound int or str

Boundary condition: an integer from 0 to 7, a Bound member, or a name such as "dct2" or "wrap".

"dct2"

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

The coefficients, a new array the shape of inp.

Raises:

If inp is not a float32 or float64 CuPy array.

Return the pointer of cupy's current CUDA stream.

fastfields_bind forwards its stream argument straight to the CUDA backend, so every wrapper passes this value. Because cupy queues all work on its current stream, forwarding that same stream keeps the binding's kernels ordered correctly with respect to the surrounding cupy operations (allocation of the output, later reads, etc.). items.title: fastfields.helpers
items.text:
Shared enums and argument normalisers for the fastfields namespaces.

fastfields.numpy, fastfields.torch, fastfields.cupy and fastfields.auto all need the same logic that does not depend on an array library:

  • the Spline and Bound enums and the normalisers that turn an integer, an enum member or a name into one of them;
  • the resolution of factor, shape and anchor into the per-axis scale and scalar shift that the resampling kernels consume;
  • the checks that decide whether the installed fastfields-dlpack is a CUDA build.

It lives here, in one place, so that each of them imports it instead of carrying a copy.

The package is pure Python and imports nothing but the standard library: no NumPy, PyTorch or CuPy, and not the compiled fastfields.dlpack bindings. That is the reason it exists apart from them. A fix to this logic ships as an ordinary pure-Python release, without recompiling the C++/CUDA chain or rebuilding the per-platform wheels. It is a sibling of fastfields.dlpack, not a layer over it, and neither depends on the other.

items.text:
anchor_scale_shift(anchor: str, inshape: Sequence[int], outshape: Sequence[int], ndim: int) -> tuple[list[float], float]

Turn an anchor into the scale and shift of the resampling kernel.

For output index loc, the kernel samples the input at scale[d] * loc + shift * (scale[d] - 1) along axis d. The four anchors choose which points of the two grids line up:

anchor scale[d] shift "centers" (in-1) / (out-1) 0.0 "edges" in / out 0.5 "first" in / out 0.0 "last" in / out 1.0

With "centers" the first and last samples coincide; the scale is 1 along an axis where either size is 1. With "edges" the outer edges of the voxels coincide, with "first" the first voxel is the anchor and with "last" the last one. The names follow interpol.resize.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default anchor str

"centers", "edges", "first" or "last", or their initial letters. Only the first letter is looked at, in any case.

required inshape sequence of int

Input and output sizes of the resampled axes, ndim values each.

required outshape sequence of int

Input and output sizes of the resampled axes, ndim values each.

required ndim int

Number of resampled axes.

required

Returns:

Name Type Description scale list of float

Input-index step per output-index step, one value per axis.

shift float

The shift, shared by all axes.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If anchor does not start with c, e, f or l.

items.title: fastfields.numpy
items.text: Every function of fastfields.numpy, with its arguments, options and exceptions. The overview explains the conventions they share.

items.title: fastfields.numpy
items.text:
NumPy interface to the fastfields operators.

Every function takes NumPy arrays and returns newly allocated NumPy arrays; its inputs are never modified. The exceptions are the functions whose name ends in an underscore, such as dt_euclidean_, sym_solve_ and spline_coeff_: they update their first argument in place and return it. fastfields.cupy follows the same rule, while fastfields.torch leaves out the in-place spelling of operations whose backward pass would need the value being overwritten (see API_CONTRACT.md, "In-place policy").

The operations fall into five groups: distance transforms (dt_*), linear algebra on fields of small symmetric matrices (sym_*), spline resampling and prefiltering (resample, restriction, spline_coeff), spline sampling (pull, push, count, grad) and spatial regularisers (field_* and flow_*). A field is a multi-channel image with any number of channels. A flow is a vector field with one component per spatial dimension.

Batch axes are broadcast. The compiled library wants every input of an operation to have the same batch shape, so the wrappers first expand each input to the common one. The expansion gives the broadcast axes a stride of zero, which makes it a view of the original memory: nothing is copied. Outputs carry the broadcast batch shape.

Inputs are not copied if it can be avoided. They are passed with their own strides, contiguous or not. The exceptions are read-only arrays, which NumPy cannot export through DLPack and which are therefore copied, and arrays of a dtype other than float32 or float64, which are converted to float64. The in-place functions never convert; they raise TypeError instead.

Spline orders and boundary conditions are chosen with order and bound. Either accepts an integer, a Spline or Bound member, or a name such as "cubic" or "dct2".

What this wrapper deliberately does not expose

Of the 58 public operations of the C++ hub, this package wraps all but four: pull_backward, push_backward, count_backward and grad_backward. They are the adjoints of the sampling operators with respect to both the sampled field and the sampling coordinates, and they exist so that an autograd engine can differentiate through grid. Only fastfields.torch has one. A wrapper here would be a function that nothing calls, with several pre-zeroed buffers for the caller to get right. They remain available through the raw bindings, as fastfields.dlpack.pull_backward(...) and so on.

tests/test_api_coverage_numpy.py fails if the set of omitted operations ever changes by accident, and tools/api_inventory.py in fastfields-dlpack prints the full matrix.

Squared distance from points to a spline, refined with Brent's method.

The curve is a spline with N coefficients in D dimensions. For each query point the closest point of the curve is searched for. The result is the pair (dist, time): the squared distance and the curve parameter at which it is attained. Batch axes of all inputs are broadcast against each other.

The curve parameter is refined by Brent's method, which needs a bracket around the optimum; step sets how wide the initial one is. dt_spline_table and dt_spline_gaussnewton are the alternatives.

3 bound int or str

Boundary condition: an integer from 0 to 7, a Bound member, or a name such as "dct2" or "wrap".

items.text:
field_cg(sol: ndarray, mat: ndarray, grd: ndarray, absolute: float | Sequence[float] | None = None, membrane: float | Sequence[float] | None = None, bending: float | Sequence[float] | None = None, *, voxel_size: float | Sequence[float] | None = None, bound: int | str = 'dct2', ndim: int = 1, nb_iter: int = 32, tol: float = 1e-08, return_info: bool = False) -> ndarray | tuple[ndarray, CGInfo]

Solve (M + L) x = g by preconditioned conjugate gradients.

The Krylov alternative to the Gauss-Seidel sweeps of field_relax on the same system, Jacobi-preconditioned with (M + diag(L))^-1 as in field_precond.

sol is both the starting point and the output: it is updated in place and returned. Pass zeros for a cold start, or a previous estimate to continue from it.

The iteration stops after nb_iter steps, as soon as the relative residual falls below tol (with tol <= 0 every iteration is run), or early if the operator turns out not to be positive definite along the current search direction. Pass return_info=True to find out which happened.

CPU only

This operation is CPU-only in the underlying library, whose dot products need a device-side reduction that the CUDA backend does not implement yet. That costs this NumPy wrapper nothing, but it is why fastfields.cupy has no field_cg.

Starting point on entry, solution on exit, shape (*batch, *spatial, C). Updated in place.

required mat ndarray

Per-voxel matrix M in compact-symmetric packing, shape (*batch, *spatial, C*(C+1)//2).

required grd ndarray

Right-hand side g, shape (*batch, *spatial, C).

required absolute float or sequence of float

Weight of the absolute (L2) penalty. A scalar applies to every channel; a sequence gives one weight per channel. None disables the penalty.

None membrane float or sequence of float

Weight of the membrane (first-order) penalty, in the same format as absolute.

None bending float or sequence of float

Weight of the bending (second-order) penalty, in the same format as absolute.

None voxel_size float or sequence of float

Spatial voxel size: one value per spatial axis, or a single value for all. None means unit voxels.

None bound int or str

"dct2" ndim int

Number of spatial axes. They are the ndim axes just before the channel axis; this is not inferred, so pass it explicitly for anything but 1D data.

1 nb_iter int

Maximum number of iterations.

32 tol float

Relative residual at which to stop; zero or negative disables the early exit.

1e-08 return_info bool

Also return a CGInfo with the iteration count and final residual.

sol, updated in place. With return_info=True, a tuple of sol and a CGInfo.

items.title: fastfields.torch
items.text: Every function of fastfields.torch, with its arguments, options, exceptions and what is differentiable. The overview explains the conventions they share.

items.title: fastfields.torch
items.text:
PyTorch interface to the fastfields operators, with autograd.

Functions take tensors and return newly allocated tensors. Most of them are differentiable, so they can sit inside a model and gradients flow through them. Functions whose name ends in an underscore update their first argument in place and return it. CPU tensors work with any build of fastfields-dlpack. A CUDA tensor needs a CUDA build; handing one to a CPU-only build raises RuntimeError at the call, naming the wheel-index lane to install.

Differentiable operations. Gradients are available with respect to the following arguments.

  • sym_matvec: mat and vec.
  • sym_solve and sym_solve_: vec (the right-hand side) only.
  • resample, restriction, spline_coeff and spline_coeff_: the input.
  • pull, push and grad: the field and the sampling grid. count: grid. grad is itself a derivative operator, so differentiating it gives the second-order terms that an image gradient computed inside a loss needs.
  • The regulariser operators: field_matvec and flow_matvec with respect to the input; their accumulate forms (*_add* and *_sub* of the product, the diagonal and the stencil) with respect to the accumulator and, for the product, the array it is applied to; and field_forward, field_precond and their flow twins, as described in each function.

Operations that are not differentiable are still exposed, for parity with fastfields.numpy and fastfields.cupy. Their forward pass always runs, even when an input requires grad; only calling .backward() through the output raises RuntimeError, naming the operation. They are the distance transforms (dt_*), sym_invert and sym_invert_, the iterative solvers field_relax, flow_relax and their *_relax_rls variants, the stencil and diagonal builders, and the gradients of sym_addmatvec_ and sym_submatvec_ with respect to mat and vec.

What this wrapper deliberately does not expose

Of the 58 public operations of the C++ hub, this package wraps all but eight, in two groups.

Adjoints, used but not re-exported. pull_backward, push_backward, count_backward, grad_backward and sym_matvec_backward are the gradients behind the autograd.Function of each forward operation. The supported way to reach them is to call pull, push, count, grad or sym_matvec and then .backward(). Re-exporting them would offer a second, unchecked spelling of a gradient, with pre-zeroed buffers and an accumulate-or-overwrite contract for the caller to get right. fastfields.dlpack has them raw.

Solver entry points that need an autograd decision first. field_precond_, flow_precond_ and field_cg. The in-place preconditioner solves would have to settle how autograd treats a mutated buffer (API_CONTRACT.md, "In-place policy"), and field_cg runs an iterative solver whose gradient is a solve with the same operator. Both are worth doing and neither is a mechanical wrapper. field_relax is the in-place solver available today, and fastfields.numpy has all three for the case without autograd.

tests/test_api_coverage_torch.py fails if the set of omitted operations ever changes by accident.

items.title: Bound
items.text:
Bases: IntEnum

Boundary condition, applied to every spatial axis.

Member Value Beyond the last voxel, the signal Zero 0 is zero Replicate 1 repeats the last voxel (coordinates are clipped) DCT1 2 is symmetric about the centre of the last voxel DCT2 3 is symmetric about the edge of the last voxel DST1 4 is antisymmetric about the centre of the last voxel DST2 5 is antisymmetric about the edge of the last voxel DFT 6 wraps around (circular) NoCheck 7 is not handled: coordinates are assumed inbound

DCT2 is the Neumann condition and DST2 the Dirichlet one.

The wrappers take it as the bound argument, as an integer, as a member of this enum or as a name such as "dct2"; see as_bound.

items.title: Spline
items.text:
Bases: IntEnum

Order of the spline used for interpolation.

The members are the integers 0 to 7, from Nearest (0), Linear (1), Quadratic (2) and Cubic (3) up to FourthOrder, FifthOrder, SixthOrder and SeventhOrder (4 to 7).

The wrappers take it as the order argument, as an integer, as a member of this enum or as a name such as "cubic"; see as_spline. The raw fastfields.dlpack bindings and the C++ library call the same argument spline.

items.title: dt_spline_brent
items.text:
dt_spline_brent(loc: Tensor, coeff: Tensor, *, max_iter: int = 64, tol: float = 1e-06, step: float = 0.1, order: int | str = 3, bound: int | str = 'dct2') -> Tuple[Tensor, Tensor]

Squared distance from points to a spline, refined with Brent's method.

The curve is a spline with N coefficients in D dimensions. For each query point the closest point of the curve is searched for. The result is the pair (dist, time): the squared distance and the curve parameter at which it is attained. Batch axes of all inputs are broadcast against each other.

The curve parameter is refined by Brent's method, which needs a bracket around the optimum; step sets how wide the initial one is. dt_spline_table and dt_spline_gaussnewton are the alternatives.

Not differentiable: the forward pass runs normally, even when an input requires grad, but calling .backward() through the result raises RuntimeError. The result comes from an inner optimisation that the library does not differentiate.

Squared distance from points to a spline, refined with Gauss-Newton.

The curve is a spline with N coefficients in D dimensions. For each query point the closest point of the curve is searched for. The result is the pair (dist, time): the squared distance and the curve parameter at which it is attained. Batch axes of all inputs are broadcast against each other.

The curve is a spline with N coefficients in D dimensions. For each query point the closest point of the curve is searched for. The result is the pair (dist, time): the squared distance and the curve parameter at which it is attained. Batch axes of all inputs are broadcast against each other.

items.title: grad
items.text:
grad(inp: Tensor, grid: Tensor, order: int | str = 2, bound: int | str = 'dct2', *, extrapolate: int = 1, abs: bool = False) -> Tensor

Sample the spatial gradient of a spline volume at arbitrary coordinates.

Coordinates are in voxels, channels come last and the first coordinate is x. For a spatial rank D of 1, 2 or 3 and any number of leading batch axes B, the volume inp is (*B, *inshape, C) and the coordinates grid are (*B, *outshape, D); D is read from the last axis of grid. The result holds, for every coordinate and channel, the vector of the D spatial derivatives.

With abs=True the absolute value of each spline derivative is used instead of its signed value.

Differentiable with respect to both inp and grid. Because grad is itself a derivative operator, differentiating it yields second-order terms; that is what lets an image gradient computed inside a loss train the deformation that produced grid.

With abs=True the backward pass is the adjoint of the absolute-value operator, which is a majorisation and deliberately not the Jacobian of the forward map.

Volume of spline coefficients, shape (*B, *inshape, C).

required grid Tensor

Sampling coordinates in voxels, x first, shape (*B, *outshape, D). D is the spatial rank (1, 2 or 3) and grid must have the same number of axes as inp.

required order int or str

2 bound int or str

Boundary condition: an integer from 0 to 7, a Bound member, or a name such as "dct2" or "wrap".

"dct2" extrapolate int

How far outside the field of view samples still count: 1 always, 0 not past the voxel centres, -1 not past the voxel edges.

1 abs bool

Take the absolute value of each spline derivative.

False

The gradients, shape (*B, *outshape, C, D).

field_forward(mat: Tensor, vec: Tensor, absolute=None, membrane=None, bending=None, *, voxel_size=None, bound: int | str = 'dct2', ndim: int = 1) -> Tensor

Apply the regularised system: (M + L) @ vec.

Computes (M + L) @ vec, where M is the per-voxel matrix mat and L is the field regulariser L. This is the operator that field_relax solves. Each penalty is given per channel and the regulariser never couples channels.

Batch axes of mat and vec are broadcast against each other; the spatial axes and the last axis must match.

Differentiable with respect to both mat and vec.

Composed, not fused

numpy and cupy call a single fused kernel here. This wrapper instead composes sym_matvec and field_matvec, which are differentiable, so the gradient flows. That costs a temporary and a second pass over the data. fastfields.dlpack.field_forward is the fused kernel, but calling it directly drops the gradient: the forward pass runs and the graph ends there.

required absolute float or sequence of float

Weight of the absolute (L2) penalty. A scalar applies to every channel; a sequence gives one weight per channel. None disables the penalty.

Weight of the membrane (first-order) penalty, in the same format as absolute.

None bending float or sequence of float

Weight of the bending (second-order) penalty, in the same format as absolute.

field_matvec(inp: Tensor, absolute=None, membrane=None, bending=None, *, voxel_size=None, bound: int | str = 'dct2', ndim: int = 1) -> Tensor

Apply the field regulariser to a multi-channel field.

Computes L @ inp for the field regulariser L, the sum of the requested penalties. Each penalty is given per channel and the regulariser never couples channels. The highest-order penalty that is set decides the finite-difference stencil.

With unit voxels and only absolute, the operator scales each channel by its weight; with only membrane it is the discrete negative Laplacian.

The *_addmatvec, *_submatvec and *_rls families accumulate or reweight this operator.

Differentiable with respect to inp. The operator is symmetric, so the backward pass applies the same operator.

The field to filter, shape (*batch, *spatial, C).

required absolute float or sequence of float

Weight of the absolute (L2) penalty. A scalar applies to every channel; a sequence gives one weight per channel. None disables the penalty.

None membrane float or sequence of float

Weight of the membrane (first-order) penalty, in the same format as absolute.

items.text:
field_precond(mat: Tensor, vec: Tensor, absolute=None, membrane=None, bending=None, *, voxel_size=None, bound: int | str = 'dct2', ndim: int = 1) -> Tensor

Jacobi preconditioner of the regularised system.

Solves (M + diag(L)) x = vec voxel by voxel, where M is the per-voxel matrix mat and diag(L) is the diagonal of the field regulariser L. It approximates the inverse of the operator of field_forward. Each penalty is given per channel and the regulariser never couples channels.

Batch axes of mat and vec are broadcast against each other; the spatial axes and the last axis must match.

Differentiable with respect to vec, through the self-adjoint solve. mat must not require grad, as for sym_solve.

Composed, not fused

numpy and cupy call a single fused kernel here. This wrapper instead composes field_diag and sym_solve, which are differentiable, so the gradient flows. fastfields.dlpack.field_precond is the fused kernel, but calling it directly drops the gradient.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mat Tensor

Per-voxel matrix M in compact-symmetric packing, shape (*batch, *spatial, C*(C+1)//2). Batch axes are broadcast against those of vec.

required vec Tensor

Right-hand side, shape (*batch, *spatial, C). Batch axes are broadcast against those of mat.

required absolute float or sequence of float

Weight of the absolute (L2) penalty. A scalar applies to every channel; a sequence gives one weight per channel. None disables the penalty.

None membrane float or sequence of float

Weight of the membrane (first-order) penalty, in the same format as absolute.

None bending float or sequence of float

Weight of the bending (second-order) penalty, in the same format as absolute.

None voxel_size float or sequence of float

Spatial voxel size: one value per spatial axis, or a single value for all. None means unit voxels.

None bound int or str

Boundary condition: an integer from 0 to 7, a Bound member, or a name such as "dct2" or "wrap".

"dct2" ndim int

Number of spatial axes. They are the ndim axes just before the channel axis; this is not inferred, so pass it explicitly for anything but 1D data.

1

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

The solution x, shape (*batch, *spatial, C) with the broadcast batch shape.

The flow the operator is applied to, shape (*batch, *spatial, ndim).

required absolute float

Weight of the absolute (L2) penalty.

0.0 membrane float

Weight of the membrane (first-order) penalty.

0.0 bending float

Weight of the bending (second-order) penalty.

0.0 shears float

Weight of the linear-elastic shear penalty (Lamé mu). Together with div it couples the flow components.

0.0 div float

Weight of the linear-elastic divergence penalty (Lamé lambda).

0.0 voxel_size float or sequence of float

Spatial voxel size: one value per spatial axis, or a single value for all. None means unit voxels.

None bound int or str

Boundary condition: an integer from 0 to 7, a Bound member, or a name such as "dct2" or "wrap".

"dct2" ndim int

Number of spatial axes. They are the ndim axes just before the channel axis; this is not inferred, so pass it explicitly for anything but 1D data.

1

inp itself, after the update.

items.title: resample
items.text:
resample(inp: Tensor, factor: float | Sequence[float] | None = None, shape: int | Sequence[int] | None = None, *, order: int | str = 2, bound: int | str = 'dct2', ndim: Optional[int] = None, anchor: str = 'centers', shift: Optional[float] = None, scale: Optional[Sequence[float]] = None) -> Tensor

Resample the trailing axes of an array with splines.

Resamples inp onto a new grid with splines of order order, along the last ndim axes; leading axes are batch axes. Give either a size factor or an explicit output shape, not both.

Which points of the two grids line up is set by anchor; with "centers", the default, the first and last samples coincide. The anchor determines the sampling scale and shift for the kernel, and either can be overridden.

restriction is the adjoint operation.

Differentiable with respect to inp; the backward pass is restriction.

Interpolating resize

resample does not prefilter its input. For a true interpolating resize, pass the coefficients computed by spline_coeff instead of the raw samples.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default inp Tensor

Input, shape (*batch, *spatial_in); the last ndim axes are resampled.

required factor float or sequence of float

Size multiplier, one per resampled axis or a single value for all. Exclusive with shape; with neither, the spatial shape is unchanged. Each output size is max(1, round(n * factor)).

None shape int or sequence of int

Output spatial size, one per resampled axis or a single value for all. Exclusive with factor.

None order int or str

Spline order: an integer from 0 to 7, a Spline member, or a name such as "cubic".

2 bound int or str

Boundary condition: an integer from 0 to 7, a Bound member, or a name such as "dct2" or "wrap".

"dct2" ndim int

Number of trailing axes to resample. When omitted it is the length of shape or factor if either is a sequence, and 1 otherwise.

None anchor ('centers', 'edges', 'first', 'last')

Which points of the input and output grids are aligned; the initial letter is enough. See anchor_scale_shift for the exact scale and shift each choice implies.

"centers" shift float

Sampling shift, replacing the one implied by anchor.

None scale sequence of float

Input-index step per output-index step, one value per resampled axis, replacing the one derived from anchor and the shapes.

None

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

The resampled tensor, shape (*batch, *spatial_out).

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If ndim is outside 1..inp.dim(), anchor, order or bound is unknown, or factor, shape or scale has the wrong length.

items.title: restriction
items.text:
restriction(inp: Tensor, factor: float | Sequence[float] | None = None, shape: int | Sequence[int] | None = None, *, order: int | str = 2, bound: int | str = 'dct2', ndim: Optional[int] = None, anchor: str = 'centers', shift: Optional[float] = None, scale: Optional[Sequence[float]] = None) -> Tensor

Adjoint of resample, along the trailing axes of an array.

Transposes the linear map of resample for the same arguments: values on the finer grid are accumulated onto the coarser one. The scale is derived from this call's own input and output shapes, so a resample and a restriction with matching shapes use reciprocal scales and the same shift.

The binding accumulates into its output buffer, which is why the buffer is allocated zero-filled here. When calling fastfields.dlpack.restriction yourself, pre-zero out.

factor, shape, order, bound, ndim, anchor, shift and scale are exactly as for resample.

Differentiable with respect to inp; the backward pass is resample.

Number of trailing axes, as for resample.

items.title: spline_coeff
items.text:
spline_coeff(inp: Tensor, order: int | str = 3, bound: int | str = 'dct2') -> Tensor

Spline coefficients of a signal, along the last axis.

Converts samples into the coefficients of the interpolating spline of order order, so that evaluating that spline at the sample positions gives the samples back. For orders 0 and 1 the coefficients are the samples. Only the last axis is filtered.

For orders above 1 only the boundary conditions dct1, dct2, dft and replicate are implemented; any other is rejected. The coefficients are what pull, push and grad expect as their volume.

spline_coeff_ is the in-place version.

Differentiable with respect to inp. An unimplemented boundary condition raises ValueError.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default inp Tensor

Samples; the transform runs along the last axis.

required order int or str

Spline order: an integer from 0 to 7, a Spline member, or a name such as "cubic".

3 bound int or str

Boundary condition: an integer from 0 to 7, a Bound member, or a name such as "dct2" or "wrap".

"dct2"

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

The coefficients, a new tensor the shape of inp.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If bound is not an implemented boundary condition.

items.title: spline_coeff_
items.text:
spline_coeff_(inp_out: Tensor, order: int | str = 3, bound: int | str = 'dct2') -> Tensor

Spline coefficients of a signal along the last axis, in place.

The in-place version of spline_coeff: the samples in inp_out are replaced by the coefficients. For orders above 1 only the boundary conditions dct1, dct2, dft and replicate are implemented; any other is rejected.

Differentiable with respect to inp_out: the prefilter is linear, and its backward pass never reads the overwritten values. An unimplemented boundary condition raises ValueError. A leaf tensor that requires grad cannot be modified in place; this is checked before inp_out is touched.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default inp_out Tensor

Samples on entry, spline coefficients on exit. Updated in place.

required order int or str

Spline order: an integer from 0 to 7, a Spline member, or a name such as "cubic".

3 bound int or str

Boundary condition: an integer from 0 to 7, a Bound member, or a name such as "dct2" or "wrap".

"dct2"

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

inp_out itself, now holding the coefficients.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If bound is not an implemented boundary condition.

RuntimeError

If inp_out is a leaf tensor that requires grad.

items.title: sym_addmatvec_
items.text:
sym_addmatvec_(out0: Tensor, mat: Tensor, vec: Tensor) -> Tensor

Accumulate a matrix-vector product in place: out0 += mat @ vec.

out0 fixes the batch shape; mat and vec are broadcast to it. Note that the accumulator comes first, unlike in sym_matvec.

Differentiable with respect to out0 only. A backward pass that needs the gradient with respect to mat or vec raises RuntimeError; use out0 + sym_matvec(mat, vec) when you need those.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default out0 Tensor

Accumulator, shape (*B, C). Updated in place. It fixes the batch shape of the call.

required mat Tensor

Compact-symmetric matrices, shape (*B, C*(C+1)//2), broadcast to the batch shape of out0.

required vec Tensor

Vectors, shape (*B, C), broadcast to the batch shape of out0.

required

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

out0 itself, now holding out0 + mat @ vec.

items.title: sym_invert
items.text:
sym_invert(mat: Tensor) -> Tensor

Invert compact-symmetric matrices.

A compact-symmetric matrix with C channels is stored along the last axis as C*(C+1)//2 values: the diagonal first, then the rows of the upper triangle. Vectors have a last axis of length C. The inverse is symmetric too and is returned in the same packing.

sym_invert_ is the in-place version.

Not differentiable: the forward pass runs normally, even when an input requires grad, but calling .backward() through the result raises RuntimeError.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mat Tensor

Compact-symmetric matrices, shape (*B, C*(C+1)//2).

required

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

The packed inverses, with the shape of mat.

Raises:

Type Description RuntimeError

If .backward() is called through the result.

items.title: sym_solve
items.text:
sym_solve(mat: Tensor, vec: Tensor, weight: Optional[Tensor] = None) -> Tensor

Solve compact-symmetric systems, optionally with a diagonal added.

A compact-symmetric matrix with C channels is stored along the last axis as C*(C+1)//2 values: the diagonal first, then the rows of the upper triangle. Vectors have a last axis of length C. Solves (mat + diag(weight)) x = vec for x, voxel by voxel. Batch axes of all inputs are broadcast against each other.

sym_solve_ is the in-place version.

Differentiable with respect to vec only; weight is treated as a constant. The solve does not backpropagate through mat, which therefore must not require grad: pass mat.detach().

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mat Tensor

Compact-symmetric matrices, shape (*B, C*(C+1)//2).

required vec Tensor

Right-hand sides, shape (*B, C).

required weight Tensor

Diagonal added to mat before solving, shape (*B, C).

None

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

The solution x, shape (*B, C) with the broadcast batch shape.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If an argument is not float32 or float64.

ValueError

If mat requires grad.

items.title: sym_solve_
items.text:
sym_solve_(inp_out: Tensor, mat: Tensor, weight: Optional[Tensor] = None) -> Tensor

Solve compact-symmetric linear systems in place.

Solves (mat + diag(weight)) x = inp_out for x and stores x in inp_out. inp_out fixes the batch shape; mat and weight are broadcast to it. Note that the right-hand side comes first, unlike in sym_solve.

Differentiable with respect to inp_out, like sym_solve, whose backward pass never reads the overwritten right-hand side. weight is a constant and mat must not require grad. A leaf tensor that requires grad cannot be modified in place.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default inp_out Tensor

Right-hand sides, shape (*B, C), on entry; the solutions on exit.

required mat Tensor

Compact-symmetric matrices, shape (*B, C*(C+1)//2), broadcast to the batch shape of inp_out.

required weight Tensor

Diagonal added to mat, shape (*B, C), broadcast to the batch shape of inp_out.

None

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

inp_out itself, now holding the solution.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If mat requires grad, or the channel counts disagree.

RuntimeError

If inp_out is a leaf tensor that requires grad.
